questions.problem:
Find the general solution of the Clairaut differential equation

$$
y=x{y}^{′}+4({y}^{′})^{2}-{y}^{′}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
To solve the Clairaut differential equation

$$
y=x{y}^{′}+4({y}^{′})^{2}-{y}^{′},
$$

we start by setting
$p={y}^{′}.$

Substituting this into the equation gives

$$
y=xp+4{p}^{2}-p.
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =(xp+4{p}^{2}-p)^{′} \\ p & =p+x{p}^{′}+8p{p}^{′}-{p}^{′} \\ 0 & ={p}^{′}(x+8p-1)\end{aligned}
$$

The product on the right-hand side equals zero, which means at least one of the factors must be zero.

The general solution of the Clairaut differential equation is obtained if ${p}^{′}=0.$ Then, $p$ is constant, say 

$$
p=c.
$$

Substituting $p=c$ into $y=xp+4{p}^{2}-p,$ we get the general solution

$$
y=cx+4{c}^{2}-c.
$$

This represents a family of straight lines, one line for each constant value of $c.$

questions.problem:
Find the general solution of the Clairaut differential equation:

$$
y=x{y}^{′}+({y}^{′})^{3}-2{y}^{′}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
To solve the Clairaut differential equation

$$
y=x{y}^{′}+({y}^{′})^{3}-2{y}^{′},
$$

we start by setting
$p={y}^{′}.$

Substituting this into the equation gives

$$
y=xp+{p}^{3}-2p.
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =(xp+{p}^{3}-2p)^{′} \\ p & =p+x{p}^{′}+3{p}^{2}{p}^{′}-2{p}^{′} \\ 0 & ={p}^{′}(x+3{p}^{2}-2)\end{aligned}
$$

The product on the right-hand side equals zero, which means at least one of the factors must be zero.

The general solution of the Clairaut differential equation is obtained if ${p}^{′}=0.$ Then, $p$ is constant, say 

$$
p=c.
$$

Substituting $p=c$ into $y=xp+{p}^{3}-2p,$ we get the general solution

$$
y=cx+{c}^{3}-2c.
$$

This represents a family of straight lines, one line for each constant value of $c.$

questions.problem:
Find the general solution of the Clairaut differential equation:

$$
y=x{y}^{′}+\frac{1}{{y}^{′}},\,{y}^{′}\ne 0.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
To solve the Clairaut differential equation

$$
y=x{y}^{′}+\frac{1}{{y}^{′}},
$$

we start by setting
$p={y}^{′}.$

Substituting this into the equation gives

$$
y=xp+\frac{1}{p}.
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & ={(xp+\frac{1}{p})}^{′} \\ p & =p+x{p}^{′}-\frac{1}{{p}^{2}}{p}^{′} \\ 0 & ={p}^{′}(x-\frac{1}{{p}^{2}})\end{aligned}
$$

The product on the right-hand side equals zero, which means at least one of the factors must be zero.

The general solution of the Clairaut differential equation is obtained if ${p}^{′}=0.$ Then, $p$ is constant, say 

$$
p=c,
$$

with the restriction $c\ne 0.$

Substituting $p=c$ into $y=xp+\frac{1}{p},$ we get the general solution

$$
y=cx+\frac{1}{c}.
$$

This represents a family of straight lines, one line for each constant value of $c\ne 0.$

questions.problem:
Find the singular solution to the following Clairaut differential equation:

$$
y=x{y}^{′}+\sqrt{{y}^{′}},\,{y}^{′}\ge 0.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
A Clairaut differential equation has the form

$$
y=x{y}^{′}+g({y}^{′}),
$$

where $g$ is a differentiable function of ${y}^{′}.$

To solve the Clairaut differential equation

$$
y=x{y}^{′}+\sqrt{{y}^{′}},
$$

we start by setting
$p={y}^{′}.$

Substituting this into the equation gives

$$
y=xp+\sqrt{p}.
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =(xp+\sqrt{p})^{′} \\ p & =p+x{p}^{′}+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{p}}{p}^{′} \\ 0 & ={p}^{′}(x+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{p}})\end{aligned}
$$

The product on the right-hand side equals zero, so at least one factor must be zero.

The singular solution of the Clairaut differential equation is obtained if $x+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{p}}=0.$ Then,

$$
x=-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{p}}.
$$

Now, let's substitute this into $y=xp+\sqrt{p}\,:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =xp+\sqrt{p} \\  & =(-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{p}})p+\sqrt{p} \\  & =-\frac{p}{2\sqrt{p}}+\sqrt{p} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{p}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the singular solution is given parametrically by

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{p}} \\ y=\frac{\sqrt{p}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

To eliminate $p,$ we first solve the first equation for $\sqrt{p}\,:$

$$
\sqrt{p}=-\frac{1}{2x}
$$

Since $x=-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{p}},$ we must have $x<0.$

Next, let's substitute this expression for $\sqrt{p}$ into the second equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{\sqrt{p}}{2} \\  & =\frac{(-\frac{1}{2x})}{2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4x}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the explicit form of the singular solution is

$$
y=-\frac{1}{4x},\,x<0.
$$

questions.problem:
Find the singular solution to the following Clairaut differential equation:

$$
y=x{y}^{′}+\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{′}),\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le {y}^{′}\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
A Clairaut differential equation has the form

$$
y=x{y}^{′}+g({y}^{′}),
$$

where $g$ is a differentiable function of ${y}^{′}.$

To solve the Clairaut differential equation

$$
y=x{y}^{′}+\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{′}),
$$

we start by setting
$p={y}^{′}.$

Substituting this into the equation gives

$$
y=xp+\operatorname{cos}⁡(p).
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =(xp+\operatorname{cos}⁡(p))^{′} \\ p & =p+x{p}^{′}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(p){p}^{′} \\ 0 & ={p}^{′}(x-\operatorname{sin}⁡(p))\end{aligned}
$$

The product on the right-hand side equals zero, so at least one factor must be zero.

The singular solution of the Clairaut differential equation is obtained if $x-\operatorname{sin}⁡(p)=0.$ Then,

$$
x=\operatorname{sin}⁡(p).
$$

Now, let's substitute this into $y=xp+\operatorname{cos}⁡(p):$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =xp+\operatorname{cos}⁡(p) \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡(p))p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(p) \\  & =p\operatorname{sin}⁡(p)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(p)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the singular solution is given parametrically by

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡(p) \\ y=p\operatorname{sin}⁡(p)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(p)\end{aligned}
$$

To eliminate $p,$ we first solve the first equation for $p:$

$$
p=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(x)
$$

This is valid only for $-1\le x\le 1$ and $-\frac{\pi }{2}\le p\le \frac{\pi }{2}.$

Next, let's substitute this expression for $p$ into the second equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =p\operatorname{sin}⁡(p)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(p) \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(x)\cdot x+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(x)) \\  & =x\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(x))\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the explicit form of the singular solution is

$$
y=x\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(x)),\,-1\le x\le 1.
$$
